checked_sources: Koelstra et al. 2012 (full text PDF, University of Geneva open archive copy of the IEEE TAC paper)
Li et al. 2018 (full text, Europe PMC PMC5867345)
evidence_location: Koelstra 2012: abstract (32 participants, 40 one-minute excerpts); Table 4 (p. 9) and the paragraph 'For arousal we found negative correlations...' (section 5.2); Table 7 (p. 12) and section 6.4. Li 2018: abstract, section 2.2.2 'Label preprocessing', section 4 Discussions. Zheng & Lu 2015: abstract (p. 162) and section IV results. Zheng & Lu 2016: abstract and section 4 (p. 2736).
quote: we studied only the positive and negative samples in SEED. The emotion recognition capability was evaluated using binary classification tasks
discrepancy: (1) Koelstra Table 4 lists only three arousal entries at p<.01: CP6 theta (mean R -0.06, individuals -0.47 to 0.25), Cz alpha (-0.07, -0.45 to 0.23), FC2 beta (-0.06, -0.40 to 0.28). So for arousal the mean correlations are -0.06 to -0.07 (all negative) and individuals range about -0.5 to +0.3; the claim's 0.08 and +0.5 come from the valence rows (Oz theta 0.08; T7/C4/FC6 gamma up to 0.52). (2) Bands: Table 4 gives theta, alpha and beta for arousal, while the paper's text says 'theta, alpha, and gamma band' (internal inconsistency of the source); sites are CP6, Cz, FC2 (centro-parietal, central, fronto-central). (3) Table 7: EEG accuracy 0.620 arousal, 0.576 valence and random voting 0.500 are as claimed, but majority-class voting scores 0.644 (arousal) and 0.586 (valence), above the EEG accuracies; the paper's significance is for F1 (0.583, 0.563) against the 0.5 class-ratio baseline. (4) Li 2018: 59.06% on DEAP is two-class valence (rating >5 vs <5), leave-one-subject-out, as claimed; but 83.33% on SEED is a BINARY positive-versus-negative task with the neutral clips excluded, chance 50%, not three-class with chance 33%. (5) Zheng & Lu 2016: generic classifier 56.73% (linear SVM on differential-entropy features, leave-one-subject-out, 14 training subjects, three classes) confirmed; Zheng & Lu 2015: within-subject SVM 83.99% (DBN 86.08%) confirmed, so 'about 84%' is right.
suggested_fix: In the DEAP dataset (32 participants, 40 one-minute music videos), the three electrodes whose band power correlated with arousal ratings at p < 0.01 had mean within-participant correlations of only -0.06 to -0.07 (individuals from about -0.5 to +0.3): higher arousal went with lower theta at CP6, lower alpha at Cz and lower beta at FC2 (the paper's text says theta, alpha and gamma). Single-trial EEG classification gave 62.0% accuracy for arousal and 57.6% for valence (F1 0.58 and 0.56 against a 0.5 class-ratio baseline; always voting the majority class would score 64.4% and 58.6% because the classes are unbalanced). Without any data from the test person, two-class valence reached 59.06% on DEAP and two-class positive-versus-negative emotion 83.33% on SEED (chance 50%; neutral clips left out); on SEED with the same differential-entropy features, a three-class classifier trained on 14 people and tested on the 15th scored 56.73% against about 84% within person. Status: set 'partially' as it stands; 'verified' once the ranges, the SEED class count and the baseline are corrected.
bibliographic_issues: None found. Koelstra: IEEE Trans. Affective Computing 3(1):18-31, 2012, doi 10.1109/T-AFFC.2011.15 confirmed on the PDF. Li: Front. Neurosci. 12:162, 2018 confirmed. Zheng & Lu 2015: IEEE TAMD vol. 7 no. 3, Sept. 2015, first page 162, 14 pages (162-175) confirmed. Zheng & Lu 2016: IJCAI-16 proceedings pp. 2732-2738 confirmed on the PDF (abstract URL not opened; the PDF is at ijcai.org/Proceedings/16/Papers/388.pdf).

checked_sources: Braboszcz & Delorme 2011 (Europe PMC abstract; author manuscript PDF with figures at sccn.ucsd.edu/~arno/mypapers/BraboszczDelorme2010.pdf, 30 pages)
evidence_location: Manuscript: Participants (16 recruited), Procedure ('keep their eyes closed', breath counting), Procedure end ('6 of the 12 selected participants reported some level of drowsiness'), Methods on 20-second epochs centered on button presses (10 s before = mind wandering, 10 s after = breath focus; four subjects dropped for too few clean epochs), Results p. 10-11 (theta 4-7 Hz higher at all sites, largest occipital/parieto-central; delta 2-3.5 Hz largest fronto-central; occipital alpha 9-11 Hz and fronto-lateral beta 15-30 Hz lower), Figure 1 legend (p. 25) and the four topographic color bars (figure page 27).
quote: 6 of the 12 selected participants reported some level of drowsiness at one time or another
discrepancy: All numbers are present: n = 12 analyzed (of 16 recorded), the four bands, the 10 s windows defining the two states, 6 of 12 drowsy, and the color-bar limits read exactly delta and theta 0.5 to 1.2 dB, alpha -0.8 to -2.2 dB, beta -0.3 to -0.8 dB. One condition differs: the topographic difference maps that carry those color bars are computed over -8 to -2 s versus 2 to 8 s around the button press (alpha: -6 to -2 versus 2 to 6 s, because the alpha difference was not significant over a longer interval), not over the full 10 s windows; the alpha map also has non-significant shaded regions, whereas all electrodes are significant for the other bands. The dB values are plotted ranges, not reported effect sizes (the site's note already says so).
suggested_fix: Keep the statement but tie the decibel values to their windows, e.g. '...higher theta (4 to 7 Hz) and delta (2 to 3.5 Hz) power than the 10 s after it (difference maps over the 6 s windows from -8 to -2 s and 2 to 8 s span about 0.5 to 1.2 dB across electrodes), and lower occipital alpha (9 to 11 Hz, -0.8 to -2.2 dB over -6 to -2 versus 2 to 6 s) and fronto-lateral beta (15 to 30 Hz, -0.3 to -0.8 dB)'. Status: 'partially' with the window nuance in the note, or 'verified' once the wording carries it.
bibliographic_issues: None. NeuroImage 54(4):3040-3047, 2011, doi 10.1016/j.neuroimage.2010.10.008 confirmed (Europe PMC). The sccn.ucsd.edu copy is the accepted author manuscript (file named 2010).

checked_sources: Jensen, Gelfand, Kounios & Lisman 2002 (abstract, Europe PMC)
Zakrzewska & Brzezicka 2014 (full text, Europe PMC PMC4047791)
evidence_location: Jensen et al. 2002 abstract: clear peak at 9-12 Hz, increased systematically with the number of items, prominent over posterior and bilateral central regions, 'present throughout the last 2.5 s of the 2.8 s retention interval'. Jensen & Tesche 2002 abstract: 10 subjects, lists of 1, 3, 5 or 7 digits, 3-s retention, frontal theta 7-8.5 Hz 'increased parametrically'. Zakrzewska & Brzezicka: Participants section; Results 'Memory load, WMC, and oscillatory activity' and Figure 2.
quote: the number of subjects in the described study narrowed down to 69 (40 women, 29 men
discrepancy: (1) Sample size: the paper states 69 participants after exclusions (81 recruited; 6 excluded for OSPAN accuracy or bad EEG, 6 near the median excluded to separate the groups), not 68. The whole-sample linear-trend df F(1,67) would imply 68, but the subgroup dfs F(1,34) and F(1,33) sum to 69 and the stated n is 69. (2) Attribution of the eta-squared values: 0.05 to 0.12 are the WHOLE-SAMPLE effects (main effect of load eta2 0.052 absolute / 0.054 relative; linear trend 0.115 / 0.106; load x capacity interaction 0.058 / 0.052), and the whole sample did show a linear increase (F(1,67) = 8.68, p = 0.004). The 'high-capacity only' finding is from separate ANOVAs per group: linear trend eta2 0.244 (absolute) and 0.186 (relative) in the high-WMC group, versus 0.015 and 0.021 (n.s.) in the low-WMC group (35 versus 34 people, median split on OSPAN). (3) Minor: Jensen et al. 2002 report the alpha enhancement throughout the last 2.5 s of the 2.8 s interval, diminishing after the probe. Jensen & Tesche's digits were 1, 3, 5 or 7, so 'from 1 to 7' is fine.
suggested_fix: ...and in 69 young adults frontal-midline theta (4 to 6 Hz) rose linearly from load 2 to 5 (eta2 0.05 to 0.12 for the whole sample); split by capacity, the linear rise was present only in the high-capacity half (eta2 0.19 to 0.24) and absent in the low-capacity half (eta2 about 0.02). Optionally 'through the last 2.5 s of a 2.8 s retention interval' for the alpha result. Status: 'partially' until the count and the eta2 attribution are fixed, then 'verified'.
bibliographic_issues: None. Cerebral Cortex 12(8):877-882 (2002), Eur J Neurosci 15(8):1395-1399 (2002), Front Hum Neurosci 8:399 (2014) and all three DOIs confirmed via Europe PMC.

checked_sources: Lambert & Peter-Derex 2023 (full text, Europe PMC PMC10317531)
De Gennaro, Ferrara & Bertini 2001 (abstract, Europe PMC)
evidence_location: Lambert & Peter-Derex: section describing the AASM rules ('Electrophysiological recordings are segmented in 30s epochs'; wake 'if 50% of this epoch consists of alpha activity (8-13 Hz) in the occipital region'; N1 'low voltage mixed frequency activity comprised between 4 and 7 Hz, replacing alpha activity'; N2 'first epoch containing K complex or sleep spindles in the first half of the epoch'; N3 'slow waves are present during more than 20% of the epoch (6s)', 0.5 to 2 Hz, 75 uV peak-to-peak on the frontal derivation; R: low voltage mixed frequency EEG, minimal chin EMG tone, rapid eye movements). Silber 2007 abstract: 'Scoring by 30-second epochs was retained.' De Gennaro 2001 abstract: 26 subjects, 'linear increase of power in the 1-6-Hz range and a linear decrease in the 9-12- and 16-28-Hz ranges during the stage 1 transition'. Aeschbach & Borbely 1993 abstract: NREMS higher than REMS 'in the 0.25-16.0 Hz range, and lower in the 18.25-22.0 Hz range' (51 sleep records).
quote: Slow waves are defined as 0.5 to 2 Hz frequency waves with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 75 µV
discrepancy: All AASM rule elements and the 30 s epoch are as restated by Lambert & Peter-Derex and Silber. Two small differences: (1) Aeschbach & Borbely's lower NREM power band is 18.25 to 22.0 Hz, which the claim rounds to '18 to 22 Hz'. (2) De Gennaro's linear 1-6 Hz rise and 9-12 / 16-28 Hz fall hold for the time series aligned to the first epoch of stage 1; aligned to the first epoch of stage 2 the pattern differs (1-7 and 14-15 Hz rise, 18-28 Hz fall, 8-12 Hz U-shaped), so 'across sleep onset' hides which definition is meant. Note the N2 rule in the source adds 'in the first half of the epoch' and the W rule is written as '50%' (the general principle is 'more than 50%'); neither contradicts the claim.
suggested_fix: Change '18 to 22 Hz' to '18.25 to 22 Hz' and write 'Across the transition into stage 1 sleep (time series aligned to the first stage 1 epoch), power at 1 to 6 Hz rises linearly while power at 9 to 12 Hz and 16 to 28 Hz falls (26 people)'. Status: 'verified' after these two edits, otherwise 'partially'.
bibliographic_issues: None. Nature and Science of Sleep 15:479-490 (2023); J Clin Sleep Med 3(2):121-131 (2007); Neuroscience 107(1):1-11 (2001); J Sleep Res 2(2):70-81 (1993); all four DOIs resolve in Europe PMC with matching details.

checked_sources: Rosenberg & Van Hout 2013 (abstract via Europe PMC; full text HTML from pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3525994)
Danker-Hopfe et al. 2009 (abstract only, Europe PMC; Wiley full text returned 403)
Supratak et al. 2017 (abstract, Europe PMC; full text arXiv 1703.04046 PDF)
Arnal et al. 2020 (full text, Europe PMC PMC7751170)
evidence_location: Rosenberg: abstract (more than 2,500 scorers, agreement with the majority score, 82.6%, N3 67.4%, N1 63.0%) and Results ('For stage W a total of 84.1% agreed with the majority score'; 'average agreement for epochs where the majority scored stage N2 sleep was 85.2%'); Rosenberg's Discussion describes Danker-Hopfe's study as '72 recordings ... a pool of 7 experienced scorers'. Danker-Hopfe abstract: n = 72 PSGs, 'overall agreement was for the AASM standard 82.0% (Cohen's kappa = 0.76)'. Supratak abstract (MASS 86.2%, Sleep-EDF 82.0%) and sections I and III (30-s epochs, raw single-channel EEG: F4-EOG for MASS, Fpz-Cz for Sleep-EDF). Arnal: abstract, Methods 'Scoring performance metrics evaluation', Results and Table 4 (DH 83.5 ± 6.4%, scorers 86.4 ± 8.0%), 25 subjects analyzed (31 recorded), five dry EEG electrodes.
quote: the automatic scoring from the DH was compared to the consensus scoring of the four top-ranked scorers
discrepancy: (1) Arnal 2020: the reference is a consensus of exactly FOUR scorers, not five: the headband was scored against the majority vote of the four top-ranked experts, and each expert against the consensus of the other four (ties broken by the top-ranked scorer), so 'consensus of five experts' is inaccurate; also the Results text gives the experts' mean as 86.4 ± 7.4% while the abstract and Table 4 give 86.4 ± 8.0%. (2) Danker-Hopfe 2009: 82.0%, kappa 0.76 and 72 PSGs confirmed from the abstract, which does not call the scorers 'experts'; the 'expert' label rests on Rosenberg & Van Hout's description ('7 experienced scorers', 'agreement between expert scorers'); the full text could not be opened. (3) Rosenberg: all five numbers confirmed; stage R, the highest-agreement stage, is omitted from the claim (no numeric error). (4) Supratak: confirmed (30-s epochs, one raw channel; note the MASS result uses an F4-EOG derivation).
suggested_fix: ...expert (experienced) scorers agreed on 82.0% of epochs (Cohen's kappa 0.76) in 72 polysomnographies; ...and a dry-electrode headband's automatic staging agreed with a four-expert consensus on 83.5 ± 6.4% of epochs, against 86.4 ± 8.0% for each of five experts scored against the consensus of the other four (25 people). Status: 'partially' as it stands (the five-versus-four consensus), 'verified' after the fix.
bibliographic_issues: None. J Clin Sleep Med 9(1):81-87 (2013); J Sleep Res 18(1):74-84 (2009); IEEE TNSRE 25(11):1998-2008 (2017); Sleep 43(11):zsaa097 (2020); all DOIs resolve in Europe PMC with matching journal, volume and pages.
